articles.title: The Road That Hangs Over the Sea
articles.standfirst: Fifty kilometres of bends above the Tyrrhenian. The trick is to arrive without a schedule.
body: The SS163, known as the Amalfitana, clings to the cliffs of the Sorrentine Peninsula for roughly fifty kilometres and stitches together Positano, Praiano, Amalfi and Atrani. It was cut into the rock in the first half of the nineteenth century, and the coast it opened has been on UNESCO's World Heritage list since 1997.

October is the month to go. The coach parties thin out, the sea is still warm enough for a swim, and the light turns lower and more golden by late afternoon. Many hotels start closing for the winter in November, so the window is short, which is a reason to go now.

Drive it only if you like driving. The road is narrow, buses take the outside of the bends, and the correct response is to wait. Everyone else is better served by the SITA buses or by the ferries that link the towns, which show you the coast the way its sea traders saw it.

Better still, walk a part of it. The Sentiero degli Dei, the Path of the Gods, follows the ridge high above the road from Bomerano to Nocelle in about three to four hours, with the whole coast laid out below.
Stay in one town and book a long lunch. There is not much to gain from covering ground.

image.alt: A coastal road curving above terraced hillsides and a blue bay on the Amalfi Coast

articles.title: The Lancia With the Rear Gearbox
articles.standfirst: In 1950 a Turin family firm built the first production V6 and gave it a body that still draws a crowd at classic-car meets.
body: Gianni Lancia wanted a car that was engineered first and styled second, and the Aurelia, launched in 1950, delivered on both. Under the long bonnet sat a 60-degree V6, the first of its kind in series production, developed by a team led by Vittorio Jano, who had made his name at Alfa Romeo, together with Francesco de Virgilia.

The layout was just as unorthodox. The gearbox sat at the rear, combined with the clutch in a transaxle, which improved the weight distribution, and the rear brakes were mounted inboard. The B20 GT coupé, with bodywork by Pininfarina, arrived in 1951 and is often described as a template for the postwar grand tourer.
It was quick as well. At the 1951 Mille Miglia, Giovanni Bracco and Alberto Maggi finished second overall in a B20, behind Luigi Villoresi's much larger Ferrari.

In 1962 the model reached a wider audience. In Dino Risi's film Il Sorpasso, Vittorio Gassman drives an Aurelia B24 Spider flat out down the Italian coast, and the car became a symbol of Italian summer abandon.
Sixty-odd years on, the shape still looks right, and nothing on it dates the car to 1951.

image.alt: A dark blue 1953 Lancia Aurelia B20 GT coupé parked on grass

articles.title: Walking to Constantinople
articles.standfirst: At eighteen, Patrick Leigh Fermor set out from the Hook of Holland with a rucksack and a plan. It took him four decades to finish telling it.
body: In December 1933, Patrick Leigh Fermor crossed to the Hook of Holland with a rucksack, a few books and the intention of walking to Constantinople. He was eighteen, recently expelled from school, and living on a small allowance. He reached the city at the start of 1935.

He wrote it down much later. A Time of Gifts (1977) takes him from Holland up the Rhine and down the Danube as far as Hungary. Between the Woods and the Water (1986) carries on across the Danube to the Iron Gates. A third volume, The Broken Road, was assembled from drafts and published after his death in 2011.

The prose moves at walking pace. He sleeps in barns and castles, learns a village's history from its priest, and takes every detour offered. The book is unhurried, and very exact about what the eye picks up when you have no deadline.
Start with the opening chapters in Holland, in winter. Within five pages you will know whether to keep going.

image.alt: Aerial view of the Danube winding between wooded hills in Hungary

articles.title: The Right to Stay Seated
articles.standfirst: In a Vienna coffeehouse the coffee is cheap compared with the table, which you may keep as long as you like.
body: In 2011 UNESCO added Viennese coffee house culture to its list of intangible cultural heritage, a sign of how seriously the institution is taken. Cafés such as Central, which opened in 1876, and Sperl, from 1880, still run on an old understanding: you pay for the coffee once and the table is yours for the afternoon.

A glass of water arrives with the cup and is refilled without being asked. Newspapers hang from wooden holders. The waiter, often in a black jacket and bow tie, will not bring the bill until you ask for it, because bringing it would suggest that you ought to leave.

Order by temperament. A Melange, espresso with steamed milk, is the default. An Einspänner is strong black coffee under whipped cream, served in a glass. A Kleiner Brauner is a short espresso with a splash of milk.

Go on a weekday in the late morning, take a window table and bring a book. Give yourself two hours. The Sperl, with its billiard tables and parquet floor, is a good place to spend an afternoon with nothing in it.

image.alt: The gilded lettering on the glass door of Café Sperl in Vienna, with a waiter in a bow tie beside it

notebook.label: The extra hour
notebook.text: Clocks went back across Europe this morning. If you are reading this at breakfast, you have one hour more than yesterday. Spend it on something without a screen.

notebook.label: A word
notebook.text: Sprezzatura. Baldassare Castiglione's term, from The Book of the Courtier (1528), for making difficult things look effortless. It is the opposite of showing off.
